questions.question: A number line starts at 3 000 and ends at 4 000. It is cut into 10 equal parts, so each part is worth 100. A dot sits on the 3rd mark to the right of 3 000. Rounded to the nearest 1 000, what is the dot's number?
questions.explain: The 3rd mark is 3 300. To round to the nearest 1 000, ask which end of the line is closer: 3 300 is only 3 parts from 3 000 but 7 parts from 4 000, so it rounds to 3 000. The usual trap is rounding at the hundreds place instead of the thousands place.

questions.question: A number line starts at 470 and ends at 480. It is cut into 10 equal parts, so each part is worth 1. A dot sits on the 6th mark to the right of 470. Rounded to the nearest 10, what is the dot's number?
questions.explain: The 6th mark is 476. It is 6 parts past 470 and only 4 parts from 480, so the nearer multiple of 10 is 480. A common trap is rounding to the nearest 100 instead, which gives 500.

questions.question: A number line starts at 5 000 and ends at 6 000. It is cut into 10 equal parts, so each part is worth 100. A dot sits exactly halfway between the 7th mark and the 8th mark to the right of 5 000. Rounded to the nearest 100, what is the dot's number?
questions.explain: The 7th mark is 5 700 and the 8th is 5 800, so halfway is 5 750. When a number sits exactly halfway, the rule is to round up, giving 5 800. The trap is dropping back down to 5 700, or rounding at the thousands place instead.

questions.question: A number line starts at 0 and ends at 1 000, with a benchmark mark at 500 in the middle. A dot sits between 500 and 1 000, about one quarter of the way from 500 toward 1 000. Which is the best estimate for the dot's number?
questions.explain: Use the benchmarks: the dot is past 500, so the number must be bigger than 500. From 500 to 1 000 is 500, and one quarter of 500 is about 125, so the dot is near 625 — about 620. Numbers under 500 cannot be right because the dot is to the right of the middle benchmark.

questions.question: Round 3 478 to the nearest 100.
questions.explain: To round to the nearest 100, look at the digit just to the right of the hundreds place — the tens digit. Here it is 7, which is 5 or more, so the 4 hundreds become 5 hundreds: 3 500. The most common mistake is looking at the wrong digit and writing 3 400.

questions.question: A school in Kamloops raised $2 649 at its fun run. About how much is that, rounded to the nearest $1 000?
questions.explain: For the nearest 1 000, check the hundreds digit: 6 is 5 or more, so 2 thousands go up to 3 thousands, giving $3 000. The trap is rounding at the hundreds or tens place instead of the thousands place.

questions.question: Which number becomes 7 000 when it is rounded to the nearest 1 000?
questions.explain: Any number that rounds to 7 000 must sit between 6 500 and 7 499. In 6 542 the hundreds digit is 5, so it rounds up to 7 000; 6 449 falls back to 6 000, and both numbers in the 7 500s and 7 600s jump up to 8 000.

questions.question: A BC Ferries sailing from Tsawwassen carried 1 962 passengers. Rounded to the nearest 10, how many passengers is that?
questions.explain: For the nearest 10, look at the ones digit: 2 is less than 5, so the tens digit stays and the answer is 1 960. The trap is rounding at the hundreds or thousands place, which gives 2 000 instead.

questions.question: Priya rounds 4 382 to the nearest 100 and writes 4 300. Which statement is correct?
options: 4 380, because the ones digit 2 is less than 5, so only the ones change and become 0
4 000, because the hundreds digit 3 is less than 5, so everything after the 4 rounds down
4 300, because the ones digit 2 is less than 5, so the 3 hundreds stay as they are
4 400, because the tens digit 8 is 5 or more, so the 3 hundreds become 4 hundreds
questions.explain: When rounding to the nearest 100, the deciding digit is the one right after the hundreds place — the tens digit. Here it is 8, so 4 382 rounds up to 4 400. Priya looked at the ones digit, which is the rule for rounding to the nearest 10, not the nearest 100.

questions.question: For a bottle drive in Surrey, Class A collected 1 268 cans and Class B collected 2 460 cans. Leo rounds each number to the nearest 100 first, then adds. What estimate does he get?
questions.explain: Round each number first: 1 268 has a tens digit of 6, so it goes up to 1 300, and 2 460 has a tens digit of 6, so it goes up to 2 500. Then 1 300 + 2 500 = 3 800. The trap is rounding 1 268 down to 1 200, or rounding at the tens or thousands place instead of the hundreds.

questions.question: At a Nanaimo school library, one full shelf holds about 100 books — that is the benchmark the students use. There are 38 full shelves. Estimated to the nearest 1 000, about how many books are in the library?
questions.explain: First use the benchmark: 38 shelves of about 100 books is about 3 800 books. Then round 3 800 to the nearest 1 000 — the hundreds digit is 8, so it goes up to 4 000. The trap is stopping at 3 800, which is rounded to the hundreds place, not the thousands.

questions.question: A campground near Tofino reported its summer visitors. Rounded to the nearest 100, the number was 2 500. Which of these could be the exact number of visitors?
questions.explain: A number rounds to 2 500 only if it is from 2 450 up to 2 549, because those are the numbers closer to 2 500 than to 2 400 or 2 600. Only 2 505 is in that range; anything in the 2 550s or higher rounds up to 2 600, and 2 448 falls back to 2 400.
